conclusions: For any two interval endpoints, the time derivative of the integrated state equals the physical flux at the first endpoint minus the physical flux at the second: d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)). [Printed p. 4, (1.10).]

At a discontinuity, the differential equation need not hold classically, while the integral conservation law continues to hold and provides the basis of finite volume methods. [Printed p. 5, end of Section 1.1.2 and beginning of Section 1.2.]
Finite volume methods approximate integrated quantities or cell averages and modify these values each time step through fluxes across cell edges. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]

Solving the Riemann problem formed from neighboring averages provides information that can be used to compute a numerical flux and update the cell averages over a time step. [Printed p. 5, paragraph following (1.11).]

contract_plain_english: The source bases finite volume methods on integral conservation: an interval's integrated state changes through the difference of its physical endpoint fluxes, including when discontinuities prevent a classical differential interpretation (printed pp. 4–5, (1.10) and Section 1.1.2). A finite volume method approximates cell integrals or their cell-volume-normalized averages and updates them through cell-edge fluxes (printed p. 5, Section 1.2). Given neighboring averages Q_{i−1} and Q_i, these become the left and right states of a local Riemann problem. Solving that problem provides information usable to compute a numerical flux and update cell averages over a time step (printed p. 5, (1.11) and following paragraph). This introductory account specifies the workflow but no particular numerical flux formula, update formula, or quantitative guarantee; practical implementations may use approximate Riemann solvers (printed pp. 5–6, Sections 1.2–1.2.1).
